Local benchmark · explicit two-oscillator control

QuTiP versus our measurement engine

Smooth evaluation agrees within the registered thresholds

This benchmark compares the same finite data operator and the same homodyne outcomes. QuTiP propagates an explicit data-plus-ancilla ket. Local arms apply the reduced measurement operator using the current lookup, finer lookup bins, or a smooth analytic resource. Input preparation, feedback and logical scoring are shared to isolate measurement extraction.

How closely do the measurement updates agree?

Smaller is better. Outcome total variation measures differences in the probability distribution. Conditional infidelity measures whether both engines produce the same quantum state when given the same outcome. Both are needed: nearly identical average fidelities can conceal different conditional states.

Worst-case agreement over the fixed six states and q/p axes; shaded ranges are descriptive, not confidence intervals. PNG · SVG

Logical fidelity and energy after common feedback

Local minus explicit QuTiP after a single q or p extraction and common feedback. Equal averages over fixed matched inputs; shaded fidelity ranges show the observed integration-grid sensitivity of the difference. PNG · SVG

These are observables of a finite-data-operator benchmark. The small data cutoffs were chosen to make the explicit two-mode comparison tractable. Agreement at these cutoffs does not certify convergence of the physical oscillator's energy or long-time decoder performance.

Runtime under matched output requirements

All six inputs and the same full outcome grid. Three repetitions at the largest ancilla cutoff in the main benchmark; whiskers show min/max. PNG · SVG

The shared input/scoring and quadrature-basis setup totalled 29.50 seconds. Per-case setup is recorded separately in the result JSON. Timed QuTiP work includes full joint-state propagation and projection; local work includes resource evaluation and reduced conditional-ket formation. Common feedback, logical scoring, disk output and shared precomputation are excluded from these bars.

These timings compare two implementations with different state-space costs. They are not a comparison of QuTiP and NumPy doing identical linear algebra, and are not per-shot decoder latency. They were measured on a shared machine after memory-related setup interruptions. Treat them as descriptive throughput measurements; the min/max spread does not capture all machine-load variability.

What this establishes

This tests whether reduced measurement updates reproduce an explicit circuit, with ancillary cutoff, integration-grid and solver-precision checks. The smooth arm evaluates the continuous Mehler wavefunction with analytic normalization; it has no new continuous outcome sampler and has not replaced the production implementation.

A smaller discrepancy after smoothing supports a discretization contribution to the tested measurement. It does not, on its own, establish the origin of the earlier cycle-6 rare energy jump. That requires an end-to-end smooth sampler and a matched long-horizon replay with substep logging.

The comparison covers one q or p extraction, finite data cutoffs, two resource widths in the main run, and six seeded displaced input states. It is not a q/p cycle, an LSTM/Bayes comparison, a temporal-noise robustness test or hardware validation. State preparation and scoring are shared, so their correctness is not independently established here.

QuTiP provides the Schrödinger evolution and harmonic-oscillator wavefunction kernel. Benchmark code constructs the GKP ancilla and contracts continuous homodyne bras; there is no packaged QuTiP GKP decoder involved. The kernel is the same one used by its public wavefunction evaluator; the evolution uses sesolve.

Data, provenance and numerical checks

All per-state metrics CSV · Full results and timings · Numerical gates and source hashes · Pre-run methods and thresholds

Reference gates require outcome mass within 1e-5 of one, joint norm error below 1e-7, final ancilla refinement below the registered TV/state/energy/fidelity limits, and stable integrated energy/fidelity on the finer grid. There are no Monte Carlo intervals: these are deterministic quadrature comparisons. Refinement differences are numerical sensitivities, not rigorous error bounds.
